claims.text: The investigated material is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3.
The starting alloy has a single-phase FCC microstructure.
The starting alloy contains a fine, relatively homogeneous dispersion of minor precipitates.
The as-built alloy contains residual stresses introduced by selective laser melting.
Oxidizing elevated-temperature exposure accelerates degradation of the alloy.
Oxidizing exposure promotes diffusional segregation in the alloy.
Oxygen-rich conditions accelerate grain-boundary precipitation of brittle Cr-rich oxides.
Beginning at about 950 K, sigma phase coarsens and preferentially localizes at grain boundaries.
Enhanced diffusion of Cr, Ti, and Al under oxidizing conditions governs grain-boundary oxide and sigma-phase formation.
Oxide and sigma precipitates coarsen predominantly at grain boundaries under oxidizing conditions.
Grain-boundary oxide and sigma precipitates generate stress concentrations and intergranular embrittlement.
Grain-boundary embrittlement can trigger catastrophic intergranular cracking.
Reducing atmospheres suppress the formation of grain-boundary-degrading oxides.
The lack of oxygen in a reducing atmosphere prevents formation of a protective oxide scale.
Reducing conditions alter diffusion kinetics so that precipitates evolve more uniformly within grains rather than at grain boundaries.
More homogeneous precipitation under reducing conditions delays mechanical degradation and failure.
Oxidizing exposure will produce thicker, discontinuous oxide or sigma-phase films at grain boundaries than reducing exposure.
Oxidizing exposure will significantly reduce ductility and toughness and increase brittleness relative to reducing exposure and the as-built baseline.
The proposed degradation mechanism is significant during long-term exposure from about 950 K to 1300 K.
The as-built alloy has robust mechanical properties.

contradictions.description: The starting material is described as single-phase FCC while also being described as containing a dispersion of precipitates. A strictly single-phase material cannot contain a distinct precipitate phase; this could be resolved by calling it an FCC matrix with a minor precipitate fraction.
